# Applied research won’t flourish without basic science

## Authors

- Jon R Lorsch<sup>1</sup> ([ORCID: 0000-0002-4521-4999](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-4521-4999))
- Lawrence A Tabak<sup>2</sup>
- Monica M Bertagnolli<sup>2</sup> †

### Affiliations

1. National Institute of General Medical Sciences, National Institutes of Health Bethesda United States ([ROR:01cwqze88](https://ror.org/01cwqze88))
2. National Institutes of Health Bethesda United States ([ROR:01cwqze88](https://ror.org/01cwqze88))

† Corresponding author

## Abstract

Three senior figures at the US National Institutes of Health explain why the agency remains committed to supporting basic science and research.

## How best to support basic science

When considering the best approaches for supporting basic science, it is important to recognize several key principles. First, we cannot predict in advance what lines of inquiry will produce information that will eventually be important in enabling an application. Second, it can be many years before a strand of fundamental knowledge – which might at first seem of interest only to a small number of academic experts – becomes critical for developing a new therapeutic agent or other application. Finally, it is impossible to predict where important discoveries or insights will take place or who will be involved in making them. Demonstrating these principles, it has been shown that the development of a new drug can rely on the work of thousands of scientists at thousands of organizations over many decades (Williams et al., 2015).

Because of these principles, it is essential that NIH supports a broad portfolio of basic research – broad across research questions and systems, institutions, and investigators. We must encourage researchers to delve into unexplored areas of biology, including working on organisms that are not ‘the usual suspects’ but could be hiding unknown pathways that might eventually be as important in applied research as CRISPR is today (Sánchez Alvarado, 2018). Who knows what secrets the banded panther worm, African spiny mouse, axolotl, or organisms yet to be found contain? We must also continue to deepen and refine our understanding of fundamental biological processes because these details frequently hold the keys to major advances in applied research. For example, recent progress in immunotherapies for cancer, autoimmune diseases, and chronic infections rely on detailed mechanistic understanding of cell signaling processes and immunological control pathways (Waldman et al., 2020).

To advance basic research on these and other fronts, we must harness the virtuous cycle between scientific research and technology development, and create new instruments and methods to allow researchers to answer novel questions at increasing levels of resolution. Recent advances in molecular structure determination by cryo-electron microscopy, for example, have propelled a number of fields forward, including the provision of key insights during the development of COVID-19 vaccines (Zhang and Chen, 2022). We anticipate that new technological breakthroughs – in areas such as cryo-electron tomography, the determination of the sequences and modification states of macromolecules, and artificial intelligence – will catalyze many more important discoveries in the coming years.

NIH programs such as the Pioneer Award and the New Innovator Award, and the Maximizing Investigators’ Research Awards (MIRA) at NIGMS, provide researchers with freedom to explore new areas of science and to change direction as their work progresses. This freedom has allowed some scientists to study the biology of organisms beyond those historically used as model systems, while allowing other researchers to use emerging technologies to delve more deeply into the workings of fundamental biological processes such as DNA replication and cell division.

To accelerate the development of new technologies, several NIH institutes and centers have launched pipeline programs to provide funding for each stage of the process, from proof-of-concept to refinement and dissemination of the final product (NHGRI, 2024; NIBIB, 2024; NIGMS, 2024). As part of its support for small business development, NIH also started the Research Evaluation and Commercialization Hubs (REACH), which help small businesses in different regions of the US move new biomedical technologies to the market.

## Supporting future generations

It is also crucial that NIH maintains its longstanding commitment to training future generations of basic biomedical researchers. We must foster their interactions across a wide range of scientific disciplines and ensure that we are tapping into the immense talents that reside in every part of the US. Once these researchers have been trained, we need to redouble our efforts to fund their research as soon as possible after they start their independent positions. We need these new basic researchers to explore new scientific territory and enable the many, albeit unpredictable, breakthroughs of the future.

To enhance the retention of talented trainees in biomedical research, NIH recently launched two programs to provide support across key career transition points. The Advancing Research Careers (ARC) program provides funding for late-stage graduate students to complete their PhDs and find postdoctoral positions, and then supports them during the early stages of their postdoctoral research. The Maximizing Opportunities for Scientific and Academic Independent Careers (MOSAIC) program provides similar support for the late-stage postdoctoral to early-stage faculty transition. Both programs also fund mentoring centers that provide the scholars with career development support.

Moreover, in response to recommendations from an advisory committee, NIH recently announced significant increases in graduate and postdoctoral stipends, as well as its intention to raise the yearly postdoctoral stipend to $70,000 (NIH, 2024). In 2017, NIH launched its Next Generation Researchers Initiative to provide better support for early-career, independent researchers. This initiative set targets for NIH funding for early-stage investigators (ESIs), which led to significant increases in the number receiving their first grants – from 978 in 2016 to 1,587 in 2023 (Lauer, 2024). Through these and other programs, NIH is working to ensure a robust, diverse and vibrant workforce of well-trained basic scientists.

Although applied research might seem to be currently in the limelight, the truth is that the question should never be do we need more basic or applied research but must always be how we robustly support both. This is what NIH has done in the past and what we will continue to do in the future.

results.result: The authors argue that scientific discovery is inherently unpredictable: it is impossible to predict which lines of inquiry will be important, when fundamental knowledge will become critical for applications, or where discoveries will occur. Drug development exemplifies this, relying on work from thousands of scientists across thousands of organizations over decades.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C4 present logical arguments about the unpredictable nature of scientific discovery, which are substantiated by the concrete example in C1 showing that drug development involves thousands of scientists over decades (Williams et al., 2015). The convergence of theoretical reasoning and empirical evidence provides strong support for this result.

results.result: The authors conclude that NIH must support a broad portfolio of basic research across diverse research questions, systems, institutions, and investigators, including exploration of non-traditional model organisms and deeper understanding of fundamental biological processes, as these details frequently enable major applied research advances.
results.evaluation: Claim C5 logically follows from the unpredictability principles established in the previous result. Claims C6 and C33 provide specific justifications for breadth (exploring non-traditional organisms) and depth (understanding fundamental processes) in basic research. The reasoning is internally consistent and well-supported by the established premises.

results.result: The authors provide examples demonstrating that basic research enables applied advances: immunotherapy progress relies on mechanistic understanding of cell signaling and immunological pathways, and cryo-electron microscopy advances propelled multiple fields including COVID-19 vaccine development.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C9 are supported by peer-reviewed citations (Waldman et al., 2020; Zhang and Chen, 2022) and provide concrete, well-documented examples of how fundamental research translates to applications. These examples effectively illustrate the principles argued in earlier claims.

results.result: The authors assert that a virtuous cycle exists between scientific research and technology development, where new instruments enable novel questions at higher resolution. They predict that emerging technologies (cryo-electron tomography, macromolecule sequencing, AI) will catalyze future discoveries.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C32 present reasonable assertions about the research-technology relationship based on general knowledge, but C10 is explicitly speculative about future impacts. While the historical pattern is established, the prediction lacks empirical support and represents anticipation rather than demonstrated fact.

results.result: The authors report that NIH programs (Pioneer Award, New Innovator Award, MIRA) provide researchers with flexibility to explore new areas and change direction, which has enabled study of non-traditional model organisms and deeper investigation of fundamental processes like DNA replication and cell division.
results.evaluation: Claim C11 describes the design of specific NIH programs, while C12-C13 report observed outcomes. However, the causal link between program flexibility and specific research outcomes is stated but not rigorously demonstrated with data. The claims are plausible and internally consistent but lack quantitative evidence of impact.

results.result: The authors describe NIH initiatives to accelerate technology development and commercialization: pipeline programs at multiple institutes fund technology development from proof-of-concept to dissemination, and REACH hubs help small businesses commercialize biomedical technologies regionally.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C16 describe existing NIH programs supported by institutional citations (NHGRI, NIBIB, NIGMS 2024). These are factual descriptions of program structure and purpose that can be verified through the cited sources. The claims accurately represent NIH's technology development infrastructure.

results.result: The authors describe NIH's commitment to training future basic researchers through new programs supporting career transitions: ARC supports late-stage graduate students through early postdoctoral research, MOSAIC supports the postdoctoral-to-faculty transition, and both programs fund mentoring centers for career development.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C22 provide factual descriptions of NIH training programs and their structures. These are verifiable institutional facts about program design and objectives. The claims accurately describe the programs' intended support mechanisms across career transition points.

results.result: The authors report NIH initiatives to improve trainee support and early-career funding: stipend increases were announced (including plans for $70,000 postdoctoral stipends), and the Next Generation Researchers Initiative (launched 2017) set ESI funding targets, leading to increased first-time grants from 978 (2016) to 1,587 (2023).
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C24 describe announced policy changes supported by NIH 2024 citation. Claims C25-C27 describe a specific initiative with quantitative outcome data (62% increase in first-time ESI grants) supported by Lauer 2024 citation. The numerical data and temporal relationship provide strong evidence for program impact.

results.result: The authors conclude that NIH aims to ensure a robust, diverse workforce of basic scientists through its programs, and assert that the proper question is not whether to prioritize basic or applied research but how to robustly support both, consistent with NIH's historical and future practice.
results.evaluation: Claim C28 summarizes the collective goal of the described programs. Claims C29-C30 present the authors' philosophical position on research funding balance, which is internally consistent with the evidence presented throughout the manuscript. This represents a policy statement rather than an empirical claim.
